new_statements.quote: ... detrenprez [dətrẽ'pres] ... drapel [dra'pel] ... PeRŠeYYR (158r4) percer [per'ser]. Wenn aus etymologischen Gründen keine Diphthonge vorliegen können, liegt es nahe, anzunehmen, dass -eYY- betonte Silben anzeigt. Folgen wir dieser Hypothese, so müssen wir davon ausgehen, dass Fevres zu einem Zeitpunkt abgefasst wurde, zu dem das Französische noch Wortakzent besaß. [fn. 227:] Bis zum 16. Jh. existierte im Französischen ein Wortakzent: Lexeme waren stets oxyton bzw. paroxyton bei Wörtern, deren finaler Vokal ein /ə/ war (cf. Klausenburger 1970, 17). [p. 185:] ... betonte Silben gekennzeichnet. Diese Feststellung indiziert den noch vorhandenen Wortakzent im Ostfranzösischen zur damaligen Zeit.
new_statements.translation: ... detrenprez [dətrẽ'pres] ... drapel [dra'pel] ... percer [per'ser]. Where for etymological reasons no diphthong can be present, the natural assumption is that -eYY- [sere + doubled yod] marks stressed syllables. If we follow this hypothesis we must assume that Fevres was composed at a time when French still possessed word stress. [fn. 227:] Until the 16th c. French had a word accent: lexemes were always oxytone, or paroxytone in words whose final vowel was /ə/ (cf. Klausenburger 1970:17). [p. 185:] ... stressed syllables are marked. This finding indicates that word stress still existed in Eastern French at that time.

Jh. existierte im Franzoesischen ein Wortakzent: Lexeme waren ste…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the word (oxytone); if the final syllable contains schwa /ə/ the stress falls on the penult, i.e. stress is on the last full vowel. In the Hebrew-script text Fevres the stressed (final) syllable is often flagged graphically by a doubled yod, which Zwink takes as evidence that this Old French word stress was still alive in the eastern French of c. 1300.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the accessible passages.
new_statements.exceptions: Paroxytone stress when the word-final vowel is /ə/ (feminine e). Boehmer 1872 (Romanische Studien 1, on a 12th-c. Hebrew-French psalm glossary) additionally notes that in eastern texts unstressed vowels other than schwa (final -a for feminine -e: ména, adrétsa, abélya) occur in the post-tonic final syllable, which is why he marks the stressed syllable with an acute in his transcription.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word stress (Wortakzent) of citation forms as transcribed from a written medieval text; evidence is orthographic (doubled yod in the stressed final syllable) plus the general Old French rule; extinct written variety, no phrase-level or instrumental information. Zwink's placement rule sentence cites Klausenburger 1970:17 (general French prosody); her first-hand contribution is the stress transcriptions and the graphic evidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Zarphatic (zarp1238, ISO zrp) = Old French written in Hebrew characters by the Jews of northern/eastern France, 11th-14th c. Every modern source opened (Banitt 1963; Kiwitt & Doerr 2017:139,145; Zwink 2017:185) states it is NOT a distinct language but ordinary regional Old French (Glottolog oldf1239; Champenois / Lorrain / Burgundian varieties). The quoted stress statement is from Zwink's monograph on one Judeo-French text, the medical treatise 'Fevres' (eastern France, after 1300). NB: the Glottolog 'descriptive bibliography' attached to zarp1238 in our source list (Kalepky 'Zur franzoesischen Syntax', Monreal-Wickert, reviews) consists of Zeitschrift fuer romanische Philologie (ZrP) items on French syntax mis-linked via the ISO code 'zrp' -- none concerns Judeo-French.

sources.citation: Banitt, Menahem. 1963. Une langue fantôme: le judéo-français. Revue de Linguistique Romane 27: 245-294.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Argues the alleged 'Judeo-French' phonetic traits (l>r, g/k, d>z etc.) are ordinary Old French dialect features; concludes 'Il n'y a donc pas de pénétration hétérogène, ni dans le système phonétique, ni dans le système morphologique' -- Judeo-French 'n'est que du français'.

sources.citation: Oesterreicher, Josef. 1896. Beiträge zur Geschichte der jüdisch-französischen Sprache und Literatur im Mittelalter. Czernowitz: Pardini.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes the Hebrew-letter transcription system of a biblical glossary (eastern Champagne) vowel by vowel ('Alef transscribiert a, sowohl betontes als auch unbetontes', treatment of 'betonten freien lateinischen a' under Bartsch's law); presupposes Old French tonic/pretonic categories; no stress-placement statement.

sources.citation: Darmesteter, Arsène. 1874/1890. Deux élégies du Vatican (Romania 3: 443-486), reprinted in Reliques scientifiques, t. I, Paris: Cerf, 1890 (with 'Gloses et glossaires hébreux-français', 1872, and 'L'autodafé de Troyes', 1881).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Philological study of the Hebrew-script Troyes elegy (1288): sections 'Voyelles atones' (half-mute e replaces atonic vowels; final feminine e still sounded, noted by shewa) and 'Voyelles accentuées. Rien à remarquer.'; diphthongs oi, ui 'ont l'accent sur la première voyelle'; the poem is in alexandrine monorhyme quatrains. Presupposes Old French stress; no placement rule stated.

sources.citation: Boehmer, Eduard. 1872. De vocabulis Francogallicis Judaice transscriptis. Romanische Studien 1: 197-220.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: On a Hebrew-French psalm glossary (late 12th c.): 'In transscriptione syllabas fortius efferendas apice quem acutum vocant insignivi, quum praeter surdum ə alias quoque vocales atonas in ultima syllaba admissas esse viderem' -- he marks the stressed syllable with an acute because unstressed vowels other than schwa (e.g. final -a: ména, adrétsa, abélya) occur in final syllables. Editorial stress-marking that presupposes Old French stress; no rule stated.
